title: A Memoizing Wrapper
oneLiner: Write Memoize, which wraps any int-to-long function so each argument is computed only once, with its own cache per wrapped function, fast enough to make a naive recursive Fibonacci instant.
keyTakeaway: A memoizing wrapper is a closure over a dictionary: look the argument up, compute and store it on a miss, return the stored value on a hit. Each call to Memoize must create a new dictionary, or two wrapped functions share answers. Recursive calls must go through the wrapper for the recursion itself to be cached.
explanation:
Write Memoize(f), which takes a function from int to long and returns a new function that gives the same results but calls f at most once per distinct argument, remembering every result. In Python write it as a decorator, memoize(func), that can be used as @memoize, and copy the wrapped function's name onto the wrapper with functools.wraps.

Each test wraps three functions. cube counts how often it really runs; the test calls the wrapper with the given arguments and reports the results and that count, so [2, 3, 2, 2] must give [8, 27, 8, 8] with 2 real calls. negate is wrapped separately and called with the first argument: if your cache is shared between wrappers (a static field, a global dict), it returns cube's answer instead. Finally fib, a plain recursive Fibonacci whose recursive calls go through the wrapper, is called with 70: without memoization that takes longer than the age of the universe; with it, 71 real calls. The last value is true in C#; in Python it checks that the wrapper's __name__ is "cube", which functools.wraps takes care of.

In C#, return a lambda that captures a Dictionary<int, long> created inside Memoize, and use TryGetValue. In Python, create the dict inside memoize, and in the wrapper check "if n not in cache" before calling func. (functools.cache does all this in real code; here you write it yourself.)

visualizationSteps.message: Four calls to the memoized cube: 2, 3, 2, 2. The cache starts empty.
2 isn't cached: call the real cube (call 1), store 8, return it.
2 is cached: return 8 without calling cube.
Cached again. Two real calls for four answers; memoized fib(70) needs only 71 real calls instead of hundreds of trillions.

complexity.note: After the first call for an argument, each call is an O(1) average dictionary lookup; the cache holds one entry per distinct argument, k in total. Memoized fib(n) makes n + 1 real calls instead of exponentially many.
